topic.subject: social
topic.title: Markets around us
topic.scope: weekly markets, shops, malls, chain of markets, wholesale and retail, market and equality

nodes.name: Weekly markets happen once a week

misconceptions.statement: Weekly markets are only for poor people.
misconceptions.why: Students associate the lack of permanent infrastructure with lower social status.
misconceptions.fix: Weekly markets are for everyone as they offer a wide variety of goods at competitive prices, often cheaper than permanent shops.

probe.question: Who shops at a weekly market?
probe.wrong_answer: Only people who cannot afford to go to malls.

misconceptions.root_belief: Appearance determines the quality and target audience.

misconceptions.statement: All items in a mall are of better quality than those in a local shop.
misconceptions.why: Students equate high price and fancy surroundings with superior product quality.
misconceptions.fix: Malls sell branded goods which may be expensive due to advertising and overheads, but the quality is not necessarily better than unbranded goods.

probe.question: Is a shirt from a mall always better than one from a local shop?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is sold in a mall.

misconceptions.root_belief: Higher price always means higher quality.

misconceptions.statement: Wholesale markets are where goods are made.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the place of sale (wholesale) with the place of production (factory).
misconceptions.fix: Wholesale markets are where traders buy goods in bulk from factories to sell to retailers, not where production happens.

probe.question: Where does a wholesaler get their goods?
probe.wrong_answer: They make them in the wholesale market.

misconceptions.root_belief: A place is defined by its primary activity.

misconceptions.statement: The price of a product is the same everywhere in the chain.
misconceptions.why: Students ignore the costs added by transport, storage, and profit margins at each step.
misconceptions.fix: The price increases as a product moves from the factory to the wholesaler, then the retailer, because each person adds their profit and covers expenses.

probe.question: Why is a pen more expensive in a shop than at the factory?
probe.wrong_answer: The shopkeeper is just charging extra for no reason.

misconceptions.root_belief: One event has one single cause.

misconceptions.statement: A weekly market is held on the same fixed day in every town and village.
misconceptions.why: Students generalise from their own local market's day and assume the schedule is uniform everywhere.
misconceptions.fix: Each weekly market is held on a particular day of the week, and the day differs from place to place so traders can move between markets on different days.

probe.question: A trader sells in the weekly market of Village A on Monday. On which day will the weekly market of nearby Village B be held?
probe.wrong_answer: Also on Monday, because all weekly markets are held on the same day.

misconceptions.root_belief: Local arrangements are the same everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Goods in a weekly market are costlier than in shops because there are no permanent shops.
misconceptions.why: Students link a shop's permanence and rent with lower prices, or assume temporary means expensive.
misconceptions.fix: Weekly markets have no fixed shops and so traders' costs are low; goods are often cheaper and bargaining is common.

probe.question: Why do people often find vegetables cheaper in the weekly market than in a shop?
probe.wrong_answer: They are not cheaper; weekly market goods are always costlier than in shops.

misconceptions.root_belief: Temporary sellers must charge higher prices

misconceptions.statement: A shop and a mall are the same thing, only the name is different.
misconceptions.why: Both sell goods directly to buyers, so students treat them as one kind of market.
misconceptions.fix: Shops are usually single, smaller places selling a few kinds of goods; malls are large buildings housing many shops, often air-conditioned, under one roof.

probe.question: How is a mall different from a neighbourhood shop?
probe.wrong_answer: There is no difference; a mall is just another name for a shop.

misconceptions.statement: Bargaining is possible in malls just as in weekly markets.
misconceptions.why: Students carry the habit of bargaining from weekly markets and street shops to all places.
misconceptions.fix: In malls, prices are fixed and printed on the items; bargaining is common in weekly markets and small shops.

probe.question: Meena wants a lower price for a shirt in a mall. What will she most likely be able to do?
probe.wrong_answer: Bargain with the salesperson, as people do in every market.

misconceptions.root_belief: All markets work like the one I know

misconceptions.statement: Retailers sell goods only to wholesalers and not to ordinary customers.
misconceptions.why: Students reverse the direction of the chain or mix up the two terms.
misconceptions.fix: Retailers buy from wholesalers and sell small quantities directly to consumers; wholesalers sell in large quantities to retailers.

probe.question: To whom does a retailer sell goods?
probe.wrong_answer: To wholesalers, who then sell to the customers.

misconceptions.statement: Intermediaries in the market chain are unnecessary and only raise the price for no reason.
misconceptions.why: Students see that each middleman adds a margin and conclude they add no value.
misconceptions.fix: Traders in the chain collect, store, transport and distribute goods to buyers far away, though their margins add to the final price.

probe.question: Why do goods pass through wholesalers and traders before reaching the buyer?
probe.wrong_answer: They serve no purpose; they only make goods more expensive.

misconceptions.statement: Anyone buying a large quantity of goods for personal use is a wholesaler.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the word bulk and ignore that wholesalers buy to resell.
misconceptions.fix: Wholesalers buy in bulk in order to sell to retailers; a family buying lots of rice for its own use is still a consumer.

probe.question: A family buys 50 kg of rice for its own use. What are they?
probe.wrong_answer: Wholesalers, because they bought a large quantity.

misconceptions.root_belief: Quantity alone defines the buyer type

misconceptions.statement: Everyone can buy the same goods because anyone can walk into any market.
misconceptions.why: Students think that access to a market means equal ability to buy.
misconceptions.fix: What people can buy depends on their income and purchasing power; markets are open but poorer people can afford fewer things.

probe.question: Two families visit the same mall. Why might they buy very different things?
probe.wrong_answer: They will not; everyone in the same market can buy the same goods.

misconceptions.root_belief: Open access means equal ability to buy
